transitivity: both — transitive (the cold congealed the gravy), intransitive (the gravy congealed)
gloss: To become thick and solid as a liquid cools, or to make a liquid do this.
examples: Leave the soup out and the fat will *congeal* on top.
By morning the gravy had *congealed* into a gray slab.
He watched the wax *congealing* around the wick.

gloss: To block a road, a network or the nose so that nothing moves through freely.
examples: Delivery trucks *congest* these narrow streets every afternoon.
The accident *congested* the whole interstate for hours.
His sinuses were badly *congested* after three days of the cold.

transitivity: both — transitive (she conjectured that he had left), intransitive (we can only conjecture)
gloss: To form an opinion from incomplete evidence.
examples: Historians can only *conjecture* what the room looked like.
She *conjectured* that the letter had never been mailed.
Reporters were *conjecturing* about a resignation weeks before it came.

transitivity: both — transitive (the essay conjoins two arguments), intransitive (the two rivers conjoin)
gloss: To join two things into one.
examples: The two rivers *conjoin* just north of the city.
Surgeons separated twins who had been *conjoined* at the hip.
His article *conjoined* two arguments that do not belong together.
contrast: You will meet this verb mostly as the participle in *conjoined twins*. For everyday joining, use *join* or *combine*.

gloss: To cooperate secretly in something dishonest, or to look the other way while it happens.
examples: Officials who *connive* with smugglers are rarely punished.
They *connived* to keep her name off the list.
He has a *conniving* smile that nobody in the office trusts.

gloss: To suggest a feeling or an idea in addition to a word's plain meaning.
examples: In American English, 'cheap' often *connotes* poor quality.
The word 'notorious' has always *connoted* fame of the worst kind.
'Thrifty' and 'stingy' describe the same habit while *connoting* opposite judgments.
contrast: *Connote* is what a word suggests; *denote* is what it plainly means. *Slender* and *scrawny* denote the same thing but connote very different attitudes.

gloss: To force someone by law to serve in the armed forces.
examples: Some countries still *conscript* every young man at eighteen.
His grandfather was *conscripted* in 1943.
The army kept *conscripting* farmers until the harvest failed.
contrast: The verb stresses the second syllable (kuhn-SKRIPT); the noun, a person who has been drafted, stresses the first (KAHN-skript).

gloss: To declare something sacred in a religious ceremony, or to devote it entirely to a purpose.
examples: The bishop will *consecrate* the new chapel next spring.
The cemetery was *consecrated* in 1847.
They are *consecrating* the bread and wine now.

gloss: To hand something or someone over, especially to an unwanted place or fate.
examples: Editors *consign* most manuscripts to a pile nobody reads.
She *consigned* her old coats to a secondhand shop.
The reform was *consigned* to a committee and never heard of again.
contrast: Almost always followed by *to*: *consigned to* the archives, *consigned to* history.

gloss: To be the parts that form a whole, or to amount officially to something.
examples: Women *constitute* nearly two-thirds of the staff.
The judge ruled that the messages *constituted* a threat.
The review panel was *constituted* in 2019.

gloss: To keep something within limits, or to force someone to act in a particular way.
examples: Tight budgets *constrain* what the department can promise.
The new rules *constrained* banks from lending so freely.
We are *constrained* by the size of the room, not by the money.

transitivity: both — transitive (cold constricts the blood vessels), intransitive (the airway constricts)
gloss: To make something narrower or tighter, or to become narrower.
examples: Cold air *constricts* the blood vessels in your fingers.
The collar *constricted* his throat every time he swallowed.
Her airways were *constricting*, so they reached for the inhaler.

gloss: To understand a word or an action as having a particular meaning.
examples: Lawyers *construe* the phrase far more narrowly than the public does.
She *construed* his silence as agreement.
Any gift over fifty dollars could be *construed* as a bribe.
contrast: The final *-e* disappears in the *-ing* form: *construing*, not *construeing*.

gloss: To complete something, especially a deal or a marriage.
examples: It takes months to *consummate* a sale this size.
The merger was *consummated* in January.
They spent the week *consummating* an agreement that had taken years to draft.
contrast: The verb is KAHN-suh-mayt; the adjective meaning 'perfect, complete' is kuhn-SUH-muht — *a consummate professional*.

ru: рассматривать в контексте, поместить в контекст
gloss: To place a fact or an event in its wider setting so that it makes sense.
examples: Good museums *contextualize* the objects they display.
The professor *contextualized* the letter within the debates of the 1850s.
Without *contextualizing* the figures, the report is simply misleading.
contrast: American English spells it *-ize*; British writing usually has *contextualise*.

transitivity: both — transitive (pain contorts his face), intransitive (his face contorted)
gloss: To twist something out of its normal shape, especially the face or the body.
examples: Fear can *contort* a familiar face into something unrecognizable.
He *contorted* himself to reach the pipe behind the sink.
Her mouth was *contorted* with pain.

gloss: To shape something so that it follows the curves of a surface or a body.
examples: Engineers *contour* the seat to fit the driver's back.
The road was *contoured* to follow the hillside.
She spends ten minutes *contouring* her cheekbones every morning.

gloss: To break a law, a rule or an agreement.
examples: Those ads *contravene* state advertising law.
The company *contravened* the terms of its own permit.
He was fired for *contravening* a direct order.

gloss: To invent or arrange something with effort or cleverness, often in a devious way.
examples: Somehow they *contrive* to finish every project on the last day.
He *contrived* a way to open the lock with a paper clip.
The ending felt *contrived*, as if the writer had run out of ideas.
contrast: As an adjective, *contrived* means artificial and unconvincing — a *contrived* plot, a *contrived* apology.

gloss: To rest and slowly get your strength back after an illness or an operation.
examples: Patients *convalesce* faster at home than on a ward.
She *convalesced* at her sister's place for a month.
He is still *convalescing* and cannot travel.

transitivity: both — transitive (the strike convulsed the capital), intransitive (the patient convulsed)
gloss: To shake violently and uncontrollably, or to make something shake that way.
examples: Strikes and protests *convulse* the capital every spring.
The child *convulsed* twice before the ambulance arrived.
The whole audience was *convulsed* with laughter.

transitivity: both — transitive (she cooed a few soft words), intransitive (the pigeons coo)
gloss: To make the soft low sound of a pigeon, or to speak in that soft admiring way.
examples: Doves *coo* outside the window every morning.
She *cooed* over the baby's tiny shoes.
He kept *cooing* to the dog until it calmed down.

ru: присваивать, присвоить; переманивать на свою сторону; кооптировать
gloss: To take over an idea or a group for your own purposes, or to bring someone onto a committee without an election.
examples: Big brands routinely *co-opt* the language of protest.
The board *co-opted* two new members in June.
Organizers complained of being *co-opted* by the party.
contrast: Written with a hyphen in American English: *co-opt*, *co-opted*. It has nothing to do with *cooped up*.

gloss: To have sexual intercourse, said especially of animals.
examples: Most frogs *copulate* in shallow water.
The pair *copulated* within minutes of meeting.
Two beetles were *copulating* on the underside of the leaf.

ru: защищать авторским правом, закрепить авторские права
gloss: To register a legal right over a work so that others may not copy it.
examples: Photographers *copyright* their best images before posting them.
The song was *copyrighted* in 1968.
She is *copyrighting* the whole series this month.
contrast: The past is *copyrighted*, never *copywrote* — the word is built on *right*, not on *write*.

gloss: To cut the hard center out of a fruit or a vegetable.
examples: *Core* the apples before you slice them.
He *cored* and peeled a whole basket of pears.
A cheap plastic gadget makes *coring* tomatoes easy.

gloss: To close a bottle with a cork.
examples: Small wineries still *cork* their best bottles by hand.
He *corked* the bottle and put it back on the shelf.
It had been *corked* so tightly that we broke the opener.

ru: загонять в угол, загнать в угол; монополизировать (рынок)
gloss: To trap someone where there is no escape, or to take control of a whole market.
examples: Two firms *corner* almost the entire market for the chip.
A reporter *cornered* the mayor outside the hall.
The dog was *cornered* behind the shed and would not move.

ru: загонять в загон, загнать; собирать вместе, согнать
gloss: To drive animals into a pen, or to gather people or things into one place.
examples: Teachers *corral* the kids into two lines before the bus arrives.
Volunteers *corralled* the loose goats by nightfall.
He spent the morning *corralling* votes for the amendment.
contrast: Stress falls on the second syllable, so the *l* doubles: *corralled*, *corralling*.

gloss: To support a statement with further evidence.
examples: Two witnesses *corroborate* her account.
Phone records *corroborated* what he had told the police.
The story ran without a single *corroborating* document.

gloss: To make someone dishonest, or to damage a file so that it can no longer be read.
examples: Cheap money *corrupts* local politics faster than anything else.
The power outage *corrupted* half the database.
He claims the files were already *corrupted* when he took the job.

gloss: To sign a loan or a lease together with someone and share the responsibility for it.
examples: Few parents want to *cosign* a car loan.
Her uncle *cosigned* the lease so she could move in.
Nobody told him that *cosigning* makes him liable for every payment.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *cosine*, the math term, but they are unrelated words.

gloss: To put your name to a bill or an event together with someone else.
examples: Both senators *cosponsor* the bill every year.
She *cosponsored* the measure with a colleague from Ohio.
The conference is *cosponsored* by two universities.

ru: сниматься вместе в главных ролях, сыграть вместе
transitivity: both — transitive (the film costars two unknowns), intransitive (she costars with him)
gloss: To appear as one of the leading actors alongside another.
examples: The two of them *costar* in a new detective series.
She *costarred* with him in three films.
He is *costarring* opposite an actor half his age.
contrast: The stress on the last syllable doubles the *r*: *costarred*, *costarring*.

gloss: To express something in words of a particular kind.
examples: Diplomats *couch* refusals in the politest possible language.
The warning was *couched* as friendly advice.
By *couching* the demand as a question, she made it easy to refuse.
contrast: Spelled like the furniture, but unrelated. You will nearly always meet it as *couched in*.

gloss: To act against something in order to reduce or cancel its effect.
examples: A pinch of sugar *counteracts* the bitterness.
The antidote *counteracted* the venom within minutes.
Extra lamps are *counteracting* the gloom of the long winter.

transitivity: both — transitive (they counterattacked the flank), intransitive (the troops counterattacked at dawn)
gloss: To attack back after being attacked.
examples: Troops rarely *counterattack* before dawn.
Her campaign *counterattacked* with an ad of its own.
The team was *counterattacking* every time it won the ball.

transitivity: both — transitive (crews couple the cars), intransitive (the units couple easily)
gloss: To join two things together so that they work as one.
examples: Crews *couple* the last two cars before the train leaves.
Low pay, *coupled* with long hours, drove half the staff away.
Engineers are *coupling* the new module to the station this week.
contrast: *Coupled with* is the form you will meet most often; it simply means 'together with'.

gloss: To flow or run fast, as blood or tears do.
examples: Adrenaline *courses* through you before a first jump.
Tears *coursed* down her cheeks before she could stop them.
He could feel the caffeine *coursing* through him.
contrast: Nothing to do with a *course* of study: as a verb the word means 'flow', and it almost always takes *through* or *down*.

gloss: To want something badly, especially something that belongs to someone else.
examples: Collectors *covet* the first pressing of that record.
He had *coveted* the corner office for years.
It is the most *coveted* prize in the field.
contrast: The stress is on the first syllable, so the *t* does not double: *coveted*, *coveting* — unlike *permitted*, *permitting*.

gloss: To frighten someone into obedience.
examples: Loud threats *cow* nobody in that courtroom.
The new manager *cowed* the whole department within a week.
They looked *cowed*, answering only when spoken to.
contrast: Spelled like the animal, but unrelated: this verb means 'intimidate'.

ru: съёживаться от страха, сжаться; трусливо прятаться
gloss: To crouch or shrink back in fear.
examples: Dogs *cower* when they hear fireworks.
The children *cowered* under the stairs during the storm.
He found her *cowering* behind the door.
contrast: Do not mix up with *cow* (to intimidate): people *cower* because someone has *cowed* them.

transitivity: both — transitive (she craned her neck), intransitive (fans craned to see)
gloss: To stretch your neck in order to see something better.
examples: Fans *crane* to see over the row in front of them.
She *craned* her neck to read the sign.
They stood *craning* at the window as the motorcade passed.

ru: резко падать, обвалиться (о ценах); изрывать воронками
transitivity: both — transitive (shells cratered the road), intransitive (the stock cratered)
gloss: To collapse suddenly, said of prices or plans, or to blast holes in a surface.
examples: Ticket sales *crater* the week after New Year's.
The stock *cratered* after the recall was announced.
Shelling had *cratered* every road into the town.

gloss: To burn a dead body to ashes.
examples: More families *cremate* their dead than bury them now.
He was *cremated* according to his own instructions.
They are *cremating* the remains on Thursday.

gloss: To make an act illegal, or to treat a group of people as criminals.
examples: Several states *criminalize* the sale of these pills.
The 1919 law *criminalized* the sale of alcohol.
Critics accuse the bill of *criminalizing* poverty.
contrast: American spelling is *-ize*; British writing uses *criminalise*.

gloss: To feel or show sudden embarrassment or fear, pulling back a little.
examples: I *cringe* every time I hear my own voice on tape.
She *cringed* at the sound of her old nickname.
He kept *cringing* through the whole speech.
contrast: The *-e* drops before *-ing*: *cringing*, not *cringeing*.

transitivity: both — transitive (she crinkled the wrapper), intransitive (his eyes crinkle)
gloss: To form small folds or wrinkles, or to make something do that.
examples: His eyes *crinkle* when he laughs.
She *crinkled* the wrapper into a tight ball.
The foil was *crinkled* but still usable.

transitivity: both — transitive (trails crisscross the park), intransitive (the lines crisscross)
gloss: To move back and forth across an area, or to lie across something in crossing lines.
examples: Bike paths *crisscross* the whole park.
They *crisscrossed* the country twice that summer.
Scars *crisscrossing* his palm told the rest of the story.

transitivity: both — transitive (don't crowd me), intransitive (people crowded into the hall)
gloss: To gather closely in large numbers, or to press too close to someone.
examples: Shoppers *crowd* the sidewalks in December.
Everyone *crowded* into the small kitchen.
Stop *crowding* me — I need room to work.

gloss: To raise money for a project from many people online.
examples: Small studios *crowdfund* almost every new game.
They *crowdfunded* the surgery in three days.
She is *crowdfunding* a documentary about her hometown.

gloss: To get work, ideas or information from a large group of people, usually online.
examples: Map apps *crowdsource* traffic reports from every driver.
The dictionary *crowdsourced* its example sentences.
We ended up *crowdsourcing* the translation.

gloss: To put someone to death on a cross; in everyday use, to attack someone savagely in public.
examples: The press *crucifies* any candidate who admits a mistake.
Reviewers *crucified* the film on opening weekend.
He was *crucified* online for one careless sentence.
contrast: The *-y* becomes *-ie-*: *crucifies*, *crucified*, but *crucifying* keeps the *y*.

gloss: To campaign long and hard for a cause you believe in.
examples: A few reporters still *crusade* against corruption in the statehouse.
She *crusaded* for clean water for twenty years.
He is remembered as a *crusading* prosecutor.

gloss: To cut food into small cubes, or in math, to multiply a number by itself twice.
examples: *Cube* the potatoes before you boil them.
He *cubed* the cheese and dropped it into the pot.
Three *cubed* is twenty-seven.

gloss: To pick out the best from a group, or to kill some animals in order to reduce a herd.
examples: Editors *cull* three stories from a hundred submissions.
The state *culled* deer to slow the spread of the disease.
Most of the quotes were *culled* from old interviews.

gloss: To curve your hands into the shape of a cup, or to hold something in hands shaped that way.
examples: *Cup* your hands and I'll pour some in.
She *cupped* the mug with both hands to warm them.
He was *cupping* a match against the wind.
contrast: One short syllable ending in a single consonant, so the *p* doubles: *cupped*, *cupping*.

transitivity: both — transitive (lemon juice curdles milk), intransitive (the cream curdled)
gloss: To separate into solid lumps and liquid, as milk does when it turns sour.
examples: Lemon juice *curdles* warm milk almost instantly.
The cream had *curdled* in the heat.
The sauce kept *curdling* no matter how slowly she stirred.

gloss: To try to win someone's favor by flattery, almost always in the phrase *curry favor*.
examples: New hires *curry* favor with anyone who signs their reviews.
He *curried* favor with the committee for months.
She got the job without *currying* favor with a soul.
contrast: Nothing to do with the food. The *-y* becomes *-ie-*: *curries*, *curried*.

transitivity: both — transitive (he cursed his luck), intransitive (she cursed under her breath)
gloss: To use angry, offensive words, or to call down harm on someone.
examples: Drivers *curse* at each other all along that stretch of road.
He *cursed* his luck and started over.
She walked off *cursing* under her breath.
contrast: As a verb *cursed* is one syllable (KURST); as an old-fashioned adjective it can be two — KUR-sid ground.

ru: травить в интернете, затравить; преследовать онлайн
gloss: To harass or threaten someone online, especially again and again.
examples: Kids who *cyberbully* rarely think of it as bullying.
She was *cyberbullied* for a year before anyone noticed.
The school suspended two students for *cyberbullying* a classmate.
contrast: The *-y* becomes *-ie-*: *cyberbullies*, *cyberbullied*.

gloss: To condemn someone or something harshly, or in religion, to send to hell.
examples: Critics *damn* the plan without offering another one.
The report *damned* the agency in plain language.
It was the most *damning* evidence in the file.
contrast: The *n* is silent: *damn* sounds exactly like *dam*, and *damning* is DAM-ing.

transitivity: both — transitive (he dangled the keys), intransitive (the rope dangled)
gloss: To hang loosely and swing, or to hold something so that it hangs that way.
examples: Wires *dangle* from the ceiling where the light used to be.
He *dangled* the keys just out of her reach.
She sat on the wall, *dangling* her feet over the edge.

ru: сметь, осмелиться; подначивать, вызывать на спор
transitivity: both — transitive (his brother dared him to jump), intransitive (she didn't dare ask)
gloss: To be brave enough to do something, or to challenge someone to do it.
examples: I wouldn't *dare* tell her the truth.
His brother *dared* him to jump off the wall.
Nobody has *dared* raise the subject since.
contrast: In questions and negatives *dare* behaves like a modal and takes no *to*: *How dare you?*, *I dare not ask*. In ordinary American English, say *I don't dare*.

transitivity: both — transitive (she darted a look at him), intransitive (a rabbit darted across the road)
gloss: To move suddenly and very quickly in one direction.
examples: Lizards *dart* across the hot stones and freeze again.
A rabbit *darted* out in front of the car.
His eyes kept *darting* toward the door.

gloss: To make someone lose confidence by seeming too difficult or frightening.
examples: Long reading lists *daunt* most first-year students.
The size of the repair bill *daunted* even her father.
Learning a new alphabet is *daunting* at first.

gloss: To stun someone so that they cannot think or react clearly.
examples: A hit like that would *daze* anybody.
The news *dazed* her for a full day.
He wandered out of the wreck, *dazed* but unhurt.
contrast: Not the same as *dazzle*, which means to blind with brightness or to impress.

gloss: To make a sound, a feeling or a pain weaker.
examples: Thick curtains *deaden* the noise from the street.
The shot *deadened* the pain within a minute.
Years of paperwork had a *deadening* effect on him.

ru: заходить в тупик, зайти в тупик
transitivity: both — transitive (the dispute deadlocked the talks), intransitive (the jury deadlocked)
gloss: To reach a point where neither side can move and nothing can be agreed.
examples: Talks *deadlock* every time pensions come up.
The jury *deadlocked* after four days.
Negotiations have been *deadlocked* since March.

gloss: To lower the value or the quality of something, or someone's dignity.
examples: Constant exaggeration *debases* the words we need for real emergencies.
Rome *debased* its own coinage by mixing in cheap metal.
She felt *debased* by the whole process.
